lessons.title: Hindi Basics and Greetings
lessons.description: Learn essential Hindi greetings, polite expressions, and the fundamental distinction between formal and informal address.
objectives: Master standard daily greetings in Hindi
Understand when to use formal ('Aap') vs informal ('Tum') address
Express gratitude, apologies, and farewells correctly
Pronounce common conversational filler words naturally
lessons.explanation: In spoken Hindi, greetings set the tone for all social and professional interactions. The most universal greeting is 'Namaste' (नमस्ते), which is used at any time of day and is suitable for both formal and informal settings. When addressing elders, seniors, or people you are meeting for the first time, you must use the formal pronoun 'Aap' (आप). As you build rapport, you may use 'Tum' (तुम) with peers or younger individuals. Polite expressions like 'Dhanyawad' (धन्यवाद) for thank you and 'Maaf kijiye' (माफ़ कीजिए) for excuse me or sorry are crucial for smooth everyday communication.

dialogue.roman: Namaste Amit ji, aap kaise hain?
dialogue.meaning: Hello Amit ji, how are you?

dialogue.speaker: Amit
dialogue.hindi: नमस्ते राहुल! मैं बहुत अच्छा हूँ, धन्यवाद। आप बताइए?
dialogue.roman: Namaste Rahul! Main bahut achha hoon, dhanyawad. Aap bataiye?
dialogue.meaning: Hello Rahul! I am very good, thank you. You tell me?

dialogue.meaning: I am also fine. Is tomorrow's meeting time fixed?

dialogue.meaning: Yes, everything is fixed. See you again!

commonMistakes.correctHindi: तुम कैसे हो? / आप कैसे हैं?
commonMistakes.correctRoman: Tum kaise ho? / Aap kaise hain?
commonMistakes.explanation: Mixing pronouns ('Tum') with formal verb endings ('hain') is incorrect. Use 'Tum kaise ho?' for informal or 'Aap kaise hain?' for formal.
Adding 'ji' to 'Dhanyawad' is unnatural in spoken Hindi. Simply say 'Dhanyawad' or 'Shukriya'.
When speaking formally to superiors or professionals, use the polite imperative form 'Maaf kijiye' instead of the blunt 'Maaf karo'.

Kripya means please and is placed before polite requests.

lessons.title: Introducing Yourself
lessons.description: Learn how to state your name, where you are from, your profession, and ask basic introductory questions to others.
objectives: State your full name naturally in Hindi
Explain where you live or are originally from
Describe your profession or work status
Ask someone else their name and background
lessons.explanation: Introducing yourself in spoken Hindi relies on simple sentence patterns. To state your name, use 'Mera naam [Name] hai' (My name is [Name]). To state your origin or city, use 'Main [City/Country] se hoon' (I am from [City/Country]). For professions, use 'Main ek [Profession] hoon' (I am a [Profession]). When asking someone else their name politely, you say 'Aapka naam kya hai?' (What is your name?).

Use the possessive form 'Aapka' (Your) instead of 'Aap' (You) when asking for someone's name.

lessons.title: Personal Pronouns
lessons.description: Master personal pronouns in Hindi (I, you, he, she, we, they) and understand formal versus informal distinctions.
objectives: Learn all primary personal pronouns in Hindi
Understand the three levels of 'you' (Aap, Tum, Tu)
Distinguish between proximate and distant third-person pronouns (Yeh/Vah)
Pair pronouns correctly with basic verbs like 'hoon', 'hain', and 'ho'
lessons.explanation:
Pronouns are the building blocks of sentence formation. In Hindi, personal pronouns change depending on the level of formality and social distance. 
- 'Main' = I
- 'Aap' = You (Formal / Respectful, used for elders, colleagues, strangers)
- 'Tum' = You (Informal / Peer, used for friends, younger people)
- 'Tu' = You (Very intimate / Casual, avoid in professional settings)
- 'Yeh' = This / He / She (Close proximity)
- 'Vah' = That / He / She (Distant proximity)
- 'Hum' = We
- 'Ve' / 'Ye' = They / These / Those
Verbs like 'hoon' (am), 'hain' (are/is-formal), and 'ho' (are-informal) agree directly with these pronouns.

lessons.title: Everyday Expressions
lessons.description: Learn common phrases for agreement, disagreement, expressing lack of understanding, asking for clarification, and managing daily social cues.
objectives: Express agreement ('Theek hai', 'Sahi hai') and disagreement
Indicate understanding ('Samjh gaya') or confusion
Ask someone to repeat or speak slowly
Manage polite conversational transitions
lessons.explanation: In fast-paced conversations, relying solely on textbook sentences can feel rigid. Spoken Hindi makes heavy use of conversational fillers and reaction expressions. Phrases like 'Theek hai' (Okay/Fine), 'Sahi hai' (That's correct), 'Samjh gaya' (I understood), and 'Mujhe maloom nahi' (I don't know) allow you to participate actively even with a limited vocabulary. When you need clarification, saying 'Ek baar phir boliye' (Please say it once again) keeps the communication channel open without awkwardness.

lessons.title: Asking Basic Questions
lessons.description: Learn the primary WH-question words in Hindi (What, Where, When, Who, Why, How) and how to construct basic inquiries.
objectives: Master the 6 core WH-question words in Hindi
Construct simple direct questions for daily situations
Understand question word placement in spoken Hindi
Ask for identification, location, time, and reason
lessons.explanation:
To converse effectively, you must be able to ask questions. In Hindi, question words generally appear right before the verb or at the natural emphasis point of the sentence, unlike English where question words always start the sentence. 
- 'Kya' = What
- 'Kahan' = Where
- 'Kaun' = Who
- 'Kab' = When
- 'Kyun' = Why
- 'Kaise' = How
Additionally, starting a sentence with 'Kya' converts a statement into a Yes/No question (e.g., 'Kya aap taiyar hain?' = Are you ready?).

commonMistakes.explanation: Do not mix question words with incorrect verb forms. 'Kahan ja rahe hain' is the correct present continuous construction for 'Where are you going'.
In natural Hindi, question words like 'kyun' are placed before the verb rather than at the absolute beginning of the sentence.
While 'Kya naam hai aapka' is sometimes used informally, 'Aapka naam kya hai' is much more standard and natural.

exercises.explanation: Responding with 'Main metro se jata hoon' answers 'how' (by metro).

exercises.questionMeaning: Person A: '______ manager sir?' | Person B: 'He is in his cabin.'
exercises.explanation: Since the answer is a location ('in his cabin'), the question must be 'Kahan hain' (Where is).

summary: Kya means what and can also start Yes/No questions.
Kahan is used to inquire about locations ('Where').
Kab asks about time ('When').
Kaun asks about identity ('Who').
Kyun asks for a reason ('Why').
Kaise asks about manner or method ('How').

lessons.title: Common Verbs
lessons.description: Learn essential everyday action verbs in Hindi, how to identify root verbs, and how to use them in simple sentences.
objectives: Master 10 to 12 essential everyday action verbs in Hindi
Understand the structure of Hindi root verbs (ending in '-na')
Form simple action statements using present tense framing
Practice common imperative and descriptive verb phrases
lessons.explanation: Verbs are action words that bring sentences to life. In Hindi, dictionary-form verbs always end with the syllable '-na' ( जैसे - jana, khana). This '-na' acts like the English 'to' in 'to go' or 'to eat'. To use a verb in spoken Hindi, you drop the '-na' to get the root form and add appropriate endings based on who is doing the action and the tense. For beginners, learning these core action verbs will instantly allow you to describe daily routines, office tasks, and travel movements.

commonMistakes.incorrectHindi: मैं जाना चाहता हूँ - बोलना चाहता हूँ जाना।
commonMistakes.incorrectRoman: Main jana chahta hoon - bolna chahta hoon jana.
commonMistakes.explanation: In Hindi, the main auxiliary or modal verb ('chahta hoon') comes at the very end, while the root verb with '-na' comes before it.
Use 'peena' (to drink) for liquids like water, tea, and juice, never 'khana' (to eat).
Direct literal translation of question words with verbs often results in broken word order. Question words precede the conjugated verb.

summary: Dictionary verbs in Hindi always end in '-na' (e.g., Jana, Khana, Padhna).
Drop the '-na' to get the root form before adding tense or person endings.
Use 'peena' for drinking liquids and 'khana' for eating solid foods.
Verbs like 'Sunna' (to listen) and 'Bolna' (to speak) are vital for conversational flow.
Sentence structure places the conjugated verb at the very end of the sentence.
